key_findings: Most 'data network effects' are scale effects; the cost of adding unique data rises while incremental value falls; defensibility is not inherent to data. Authors list verticalization, go-to-market, account control and brand as better sources of defensibility. Allows exceptions when data is proprietary and hard to access.
key_quote_with_page: 'There generally isn't an inherent network effect that comes from merely having more data.' (a16z web page, accessed 2026-11-14)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: challenges: data scale does not create a durable moat for startups; for incumbents the owned workflow and brand matter
notes: Written for enterprise startups in 2019, before LLMs; later commentary says dated. Pairs with Bain's 'your data is your moat' (G01).

authors: Gundlach, H.; Lynch, J.; Mertens, M.; Thompson, N.
title: The price of progress: Price performance and the future of AI
method_and_data: Dataset from Artificial Analysis and Epoch AI of historical API prices and benchmark performance.
key_findings: Price for a given benchmark level fell about 5x to 10x per year for frontier models; algorithmic efficiency about 3x per year; but the price of running frontier models rises 3x to 18x per year because of bigger models and reasoning demands.
key_quote_with_page: "the price of running frontier models is rising between 3x to 18x per year due to bigger models and larger reasoning demands" (abstract, formula rendered as plain text)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: both cost decline (Canva: cost per task cut about 90%; Figma: 2x credits at same price) and cost pressure (Figma gross margin) are true at once
notes: Resolves an apparent contradiction in the cases: costs per fixed capability fall, but demand shifts to frontier and agentic usage, so total cost per user can rise. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

authors: Cottier, B.; Snodin, B.; Owen, D.; Adamczewski, T. (Epoch AI)
title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks
method_and_data: [V-open: https://epoch.ai/data-insights/ai-inference-price-trends, accessed 2026-11-14]
key_findings: The price to reach a fixed performance fell 9x to 900x per year depending on milestone; 40x per year for GPT-4-level PhD science questions; fastest drops in the last year.
key_quote_with_page: "The rate of decline varies dramatically depending on the performance milestone, ranging from 9x to 900x per year." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: cost-plus credits mechanically erode revenue unless usage grows (BCG), but a vendor tied to frontier models does not see the full decline
notes: Research-institute data insight, public methodology. Note the later Epoch update reported by press (13x per year on GPQA) was not opened.

authors: Kapoor, S.; Stroebl, B.; Siegel, Z. S.; Nadgir, N.; Narayanan, A.
title: AI agents that matter
method_and_data: Analysis of agent benchmarks and evaluation practice; joint cost-accuracy optimisation.
key_findings: State-of-the-art agents are 'needlessly complex and costly' because benchmarks ignore cost; cost and accuracy should be optimised jointly.
key_quote_with_page: "SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly" (abstract)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: agent work has variable and large cost per task (Figma agent 300+ credits for a 5-screen flow), so metering effort is rational
notes: Gives academic grounding to why agent runs are metered by work. Preprint.

title: From tokens to credits to outcomes: Pricing AI across models, applications, and cloud platforms
method_and_data: Source-traceable coding of public pricing pages for the Forbes AI 50 (2026), cloud platforms and 9 distinctive designs; taxonomy of pricing primitives and credit mechanics.
key_findings: Subscription with usage quota is the dominant observable model among AI-native firms (55% of observable rows; 45-61% in sensitivity analyses); 23 of 52 AI-native rows publish no pricing; hybrids are compositions of anchor, allowance mechanism and billable unit; seat pricing is supplemented, 'in rare cases replaced'.
key_quote_with_page: "Traditional SaaS charged per seat because serving one more user cost almost nothing. Model inference has non-zero marginal cost" (abstract)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: seat anchor plus quota is the modal design, outcome pricing rare
notes: The closest academic-style empirical study of AI pricing found; a single-author preprint; the author states that his employer (not named in the abstract) is excluded from the sample. Read in full. The register's claim of no empirical study after Saltan & Smolander (2021) needs updating.

title: AI tokenomics: The economics of tokens, computation, and pricing in foundation models
method_and_data: Conceptual framework linking token costs, workflow production functions and market design.
key_findings: Token expenditure and economic value are distinct: value depends on marginal productivity, workflow position, hidden reasoning and risk.
key_quote_with_page: "token expenditure and economic value are distinct" (abstract)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: cost metering (tokens) is not value capture
notes: Conceptual preprint; use only for the cost/value distinction.

authors: Chen, Y.; Chen, J.; He, C.; Li, Y.; Ji, Y.; Wu, Y.
title: Token economics for LLM agents: A dual-view study from computing and economics

key_findings: Tokens as production factors, exchange medium and unit of account; principal-agent and transaction-cost framing at multi-agent level.

authors: Zhuang, B.; Qiao, J.; Liu, M.; Yu, M.; Hong, P.; Li, R.
title: Beyond benchmarks: The economics of AI inference

stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: neutral
notes: Low priority; engineering-economics viewpoint on marginal cost of inference.

title: The new business of AI (and how it's different from traditional software)
method_and_data: Investor essay based on anecdotal financial data from portfolio AI companies (authors say 'anecdotally').
key_findings: AI companies often show gross margins of 50-60% versus 60-80%+ for SaaS, because of cloud infrastructure and human support; they look like a mix of software and services; scaling hampered by edge cases; weaker moats.
key_quote_with_page: "gross margins often in the 50-60% range - well below the 60-80%+ benchmark for comparable SaaS businesses" (web page, no pagination)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: variable cost undermines the 'produced once, sold many times' property
notes: Pre-LLM (2020, ML models), so evidence is on earlier AI, not generative. Foundational for the 'AI gross margin debate'. Compare with Figma non-GAAP 92% to 82% (still above 60-80% SaaS range at the top).

title: The state of AI 2025
method_and_data: Investor benchmark report with archetypes ('Supernovas', 'Shooting Stars') from a sample of high-growth AI start-ups (sample size not stated on the page read).
key_findings: Supernovas: about 25% average gross margin (often negative), $40M year-1 ARR, $1.13M ARR per FTE. Shooting Stars: about 60% gross margin, about $3M year-1 ARR, $164K ARR per FTE; AI incumbents' switching-cost moats are degrading.
key_quote_with_page: "On average, these AI Supernovas have only 25% gross margins, often trading distribution for profit in the short term." (web page, no pagination)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: AI-native firms run lower gross margins than SaaS, trading margin for growth
notes: Gamma (self-reported profitable, about 50 staff) resembles neither archetype strictly. Averages not medians; methodology thin.

authors: SaaStr (summary of ICONIQ Growth, 2025 State of AI report)
title: The age of AI: What ~300 high-growth B2B startups are doing with AI
verification: [V-open: https://www.saastr.com/what-300-of-the-highest-growth-b2b-startups-are-doing-with-ai-the-latest-from-iconiq/, accessed 2026-11-14] (secondary summary; ICONIQ primary not opened)
method_and_data: Summary of ICONIQ's April 2025 survey of 300 executives at software firms building AI products (32% AI-native, 37% AI-enabled new products, 31% adding AI to existing products).
key_findings: Pricing: 38% hybrid, 36% subscription or seat-based, 19% usage-based, 6% outcome-based; AI-enabled firms: 40% include AI in premium tiers, 33% at no extra cost, 21% separate usage-based; 37% plan to change AI pricing within 12 months; one respondent: power users 'result in negative margins considering LLM API costs'.
key_quote_with_page: "The subscription model is not working for us. Power users tend to use a lot resulting in negative margins considering LLM API costs." (respondent quoted in SaaStr summary, web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: seat anchor plus tiering is the AI-enabled default; outcome pricing about 6%
notes: Prefer the ICONIQ primary when accessible (iconiqcapital.com did not open from WebFetch). BCG also cites the ICONIQ 2025 survey (68% charge separately or include AI in premium tiers).

title: State of AI bi-annual snapshot (January 2026)
method_and_data: Survey of executives at software companies building AI products (Q4 2025 wave, about 300 per the 2026 report).
key_findings: 58% still include a subscription or platform component; consumption-based 35% and outcome-based 18% pricing; 37% plan to change AI pricing; outcome experiments mostly tie to cost savings (36%) or revenue generated (18%); expected gross margin about 52% in 2026.
key_quote_with_page: "AI pricing remains an unsettled dimension across the market." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: mixed: outcome-based pricing is growing fast from a low base (6% to 18% in about 9 months) but definitions are loose
notes: Compare with Bain's warning that 'outcome-based' labels often cover output meters (PR049).

title: 2026 State of AI report: The builder's economy
method_and_data: Proprietary Q2 2026 survey of about 300 executives at software companies building AI products, compared with a Q4 2025 wave.
key_findings: AI products grew from 32% of revenue (2025) to a projected 42% (2026); gross margin on AI 45% (2025), projected 53% (2026), 59% (2027); consumption pricing 35% to 42% and outcome-based 18% to 23% in six months; companies blend 1.7 pricing models; two-thirds report improved per-query unit economics.
key_quote_with_page: "Gross margins are improving, jumping from 45% in 2025 to a projected 53% in 2026, and 59% in 2027." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: margin compression is expected to ease; hybrid is the norm; outcome rising
notes: Self-selected, investor-run, not representative of creation SaaS incumbents. Projections are respondents' expectations.

title: 2025 state of B2B monetization
verification: [V-open: free excerpt, accessed 2026-11-14; the full 35-page report is paywalled]
method_and_data: Survey of more than 240 software companies (50% mostly SaaS, 14% AI-native, 36% hybrid; 57% US).
key_findings: Hybrid pricing up from 27% to 41% in 12 months; flat-fee down 29% to 22%; seat-based down 21% to 15%; outcome-based 'out of reach for 95% of the market' (5% primary model, 25% expect by 2028 per search summary); internal costs and margins are the most important factor in AI pricing; 53% include AI in the core offering.
key_quote_with_page: "Hybrid pricing doesn't require reinventing the wheel - it can be layered into existing seat-based and subscription models." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: hybrid layering over seats; cost-driven AI pricing; outcome rare
notes: Newsletter survey (self-selected readers), sponsored by a billing vendor (Metronome supports Growth Unhinged). Lists four reasons hybrid is popular: minimal disruption, upsell path, margins (capping usage), predictability.

title: The state of B2B monetization in 2026
verification: [V-open: free excerpt, accessed 2026-11-14; full report paywalled]
method_and_data: Survey of more than 230 software companies (32% mostly SaaS, 15% AI-native, 43% hybrid).
key_findings: 37% hybrid (25% a year earlier); largest SaaS companies change pricing most; AI credit adoption 29%, 33% plan credits in 6-12 months, credit models grew 126% in 2025; median target AI gross margin about 50%, only 12% aim for 80%+; 54% cite internal costs and margins as the most important AI pricing factor; 70% say AI is funded from software budgets; top 10% of power users drive 70%+ of token consumption (author's experience); Canva and Figma named among big pricing changes in early 2026.
key_quote_with_page: "AI credits are great for vendors. They can become a nightmare for customers" (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: credits as vendor-side cost control; median AI margin target 50%
notes: Strong practitioner evidence for proposition P1. The 'top 10% drive 70%' is an experience claim, not survey data. A mention that HubSpot 'cut Fin's pricing in half' is ambiguous in the excerpt; do not use.

title: The rise of AI credits: Why cost-plus credit models work (until they don't)
method_and_data: Vendor (billing platform) analysis with unattributed practitioner interviews.
key_findings: Teams adopt cost-plus credits because costs are known and value unknown; credits normalise volatile LLM usage into prepayment; they are 'a bridge solution' and 'useful but not loved'; customers do not understand what a credit buys.
key_quote_with_page: "We don't love credits, but we didn't have time to define outcomes. This was the fastest way to ship." (head of product monetization, quoted; web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: credits are cost control first, value capture later
notes: Vendor content: quotes anonymous, so treat as illustrative. Still the clearest articulation of credits as cost-plus bridge.

title: 2026 trends from cataloging 50 AI pricing models
method_and_data: Catalogue of more than 50 AI companies' pricing and credit models.
key_findings: Hybrid is the norm; credits serve three functions (compute proxies, abstracted value bundles, access gating); consumer and API pricing split; Windsurf replaced credits with fixed quotas for predictability; Lovable fixed monthly credit pool.
key_quote_with_page: "credits are used in three primary ways: ... Compute proxies ... Abstracted value bundles ... Access gating" (paraphrase of web page; check exact wording)
theory_or_lens: "Nearly every category in the Pricing Index features some version of a credit model." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: credits are heterogeneous: Adobe/Canva/Figma are mostly compute proxy plus access gating
notes: Taxonomy is useful for coding the cases. Vendor-run index, selection not random.

title: Per-seat software pricing isn't dead, but new models are gaining steam
method_and_data: Analysis of more than 30 SaaS vendors (excluding AI-native) adding GenAI features.
key_findings: About 35% simply raised per-seat prices bundling AI (e.g. Zoom); about 65% added an AI meter on top of seats (Adobe, Salesforce); none exclusively monetise AI as a separate add-on or fully shifted to usage or outcome pricing; AI changes both value (headcount-based meter loses relevance) and cost (inference, fine-tuning, R&D).
key_quote_with_page: "None of these 30-plus vendors now exclusively monetize AI as a separate add-on ... And none of these vendors have fully shifted to AI usage- or outcome-based pricing" (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: incumbents layer meters on seats; Adobe classified in the hybrid group
notes: Directly confirms the pattern in the cases. Sample of 30 is small; Bain says it excluded AI-native firms.

title: AI pricing: A reality check on effort, usage, and outcomes
method_and_data: Analysis of public pricing of about 200 B2B SaaS firms (June 2026).
key_findings: Among AI-native and seat-based SaaS firms adding a hybrid AI meter only about 10% use outcome meters, about 35% effort, about 55% output; about 4 in 5 vendors choose capacity (not direct usage) models, e.g. Atlassian Rovo credits, ServiceNow Now Assist, Adobe Firefly credits; outcome pricing needs outcomes that are observable, uniquely attributable and contractible, and has found a home in customer support (Zendesk, Sierra, Fin, Decagon); about one in five AI-native firms still rely mostly on per-seat pricing.
key_quote_with_page: "Outcome-based pricing works when three conditions exist: The outcome is observable. The outcome is uniquely attributable to the AI. The outcome is contractible between buyer and seller." (web page)
theory_or_lens: Pricing typology (effort, output, outcome; usage vs capacity)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: seats stay as anchor; credits are capacity models; outcome limited to support
notes: The most useful single source for the rival hypothesis. Typology lets the thesis code Adobe (output), Gamma agent (effort), Figma agent (effort), and explains why creative tools fail the three conditions.

authors: Boston Consulting Group (Dharani, N.; Pineda, J.; Andeyro, A.; Hamming, N.; Kim, Y.; Misra, N.; Bhatia, A.)
title: Rethinking B2B software pricing in the agentic AI era
method_and_data: Consulting analysis drawing on a BCG IT buyers survey and cited third-party surveys (a16z, ICONIQ).
key_findings: 40% of buyers cite seat reduction as the primary lever to cut software spend; barriers to outcome pricing per an a16z survey: 47% cannot define outcomes, 36% cost predictability, 25% attribution, 24% factors outside vendor control; one vendor shows margin variance above 70 percentage points across accounts; cost-plus pricing undermines predictability and, as model costs fall, revenues erode unless usage grows; five agentic pricing models.
key_quote_with_page: "as model costs decline over time ... revenues may erode in parallel unless usage grows exponentially" (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: cost-plus credits are fragile; outcome pricing blocked by measurement
notes: Upgrades register G09 (previously V-snippet, 403) to V-open. The a16z survey figures are second-hand through BCG; original not found. G10 (2026 BCG piece) was not reopened.

authors: Simon-Kucher (Tambawala, A.; Nepveux, A.; Ammer, A.)
title: A how-to guide to monetizing GenAI and AI agents
venue_or_publisher: Simon-Kucher white paper (uses Global Software Study 2025, n = 516 executives)
method_and_data: White paper using the Global Software Study 2025 (516 B2B software executives, 161 buyers per search summary).
key_findings: 76% of firms launched AI features but revenue impact mostly 0-10%; AI agents pricing today: seat-based 41%, fixed fee 30%, usage-based 23%, outcome-based 7%; 45% plan two or more AI monetization models; add-on options: premium plan bundling 42%, seat add-ons 41%, usage add-ons 39%, outcome add-ons 35%.
key_quote_with_page: "Outcome-based pricing is only at 7%. It's the least common today" (PDF text)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: outcome is least common; seat still largest even for AI agents
notes: Statements of 'plan to use' (35% outcome add-ons) versus actual (7%) show an intention-adoption gap. Consultancy has a stake in selling pricing work.

title: The pricing split: Why core software and AI can't share one commercial model
method_and_data: Futurum 2H 2026 Enterprise Software Decision-Makers Survey plus ETR spending-intention data (Oct 2025 to Jul 2026).
key_findings: Buyers rank per-seat last for core software (12.6%, behind consumption 28.9% and outcome 22.2%) but first for AI functionality billed separately (42.3%, ahead of consumption 36.6% and outcomes 21.1%); Zendesk, Intercom, Decagon pure outcome; Salesforce, Adobe, Pegasystems, ServiceNow hybrid; ETR net score does not reward pure outcome vendors.
key_quote_with_page: "Per-Seat Pricing Ranks Last for Core Software and First for AI, Among the Same Buyers in the Same Survey" (key points, PDF)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: challenges: buyers want seat predictability for AI add-ons, contra 'seats are dead'
notes: Buyer-side counter-evidence to vendor surveys. Futurum is an analyst firm; sample size not shown in the extract.

title: You are not a model. Don't price per token.
method_and_data: Investor essay with a survey of 50 technical AI buyers (27 prefer credits tied to recognizable work, 14 prefer tokens).
key_findings: Price at the highest layer of value one can reliably measure, attribute and defend; credits should map to recognizable work, not hide tokens; well-designed credits protect gross margins because each AI user brings inference cost; token pricing imports the provider's cost structure and anchors value to a falling unit.
key_quote_with_page: "a credit is a currency, not a value metric. What matters is what the credit buys." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: mixed: endorses credits for the middle of the stack (the cases' position) and outcome pricing only where attributable
notes: Small buyer sample (n=50). Explicit statement that credits serve both usability and margin protection supports the cost-cap reading of the cases. Written by investors in AI companies.

title: Zendesk first in CX industry to offer outcome-based pricing for AI agents
method_and_data: Company announcement.
key_findings: Zendesk charges for AI agents based on automated resolutions, with an in-product dashboard of resolutions and automation rate.
key_quote_with_page: "Outcome-Based Pricing for AI agents, focusing on automated resolutions that deliver real value to customers" (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: supports: outcome pricing exists where resolutions are countable
notes: Vendor marketing claim ('first'). Per-resolution price levels in third-party guides were not verified against Zendesk's pricing page.

title: Fin AI Agent overview and pricing (help article 8205718; fin.ai/pricing)
method_and_data: Company documentation.
key_findings: Fin charges $0.99 per outcome (resolution, procedure handoff, disqualification), one outcome per conversation; a resolution counts when the customer confirms or exits without requesting further help (assumed resolution); hard limits and alerts configurable.
key_quote_with_page: "Only pay when Fin resolves the issue end to end" (fin.ai/pricing) and "(assumed resolution)" (help article)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: mixed: outcome pricing, but the outcome definition includes assumed resolution, the measurement problem Bain flags
notes: Key: even the flagship case defines an outcome by the customer's silence. Earlier $1.90 per resolution reported by a secondary source (Sacra) was not verified.

title: HubSpot's Customer Agent and Prospecting Agent: Now you pay when the task is complete
method_and_data: Company announcement.
key_findings: From 14 April 2026 Customer Agent moves from $1.00 per conversation to $0.50 per resolved conversation (50 credits); Prospecting Agent $1 per lead recommended (100 credits), paid in HubSpot Credits; 65% of conversations resolved; claim that most AI tools are not priced on outcomes because they cannot promise consistent results.
key_quote_with_page: "Most AI tools aren't priced on outcomes because they can't promise consistent results." (web page)
stance(supports/challenges/mixed/neutral: mixed: outcome pricing denominated in credits, i.e. outcome and credit logic merge
notes: Illustrates that outcome pricing is implemented through a credit ledger, reducing the distinction between P1 and the rival.

title: Agentforce pricing
method_and_data: Company pricing page.
key_findings: Conversations $2 each; Flex Credits (an Agentforce action costs 20 credits, example 40 credits = US$0.20, implying US$0.005 per credit); Agentforce User License $5 per user per month requiring Flex Credits; Agentforce Coworker $50 per user per month; four buying models.
